name: KMP String Matching
description: Preprocesses the pattern into an LPS table (longest proper prefix that is also a suffix) so every text character is examined once. Total search time is O(n + m) with no backtracking.
explanation:
What it is

Knuth-Morris-Pratt answers the question naive search cannot: after a mismatch, how much of the pattern still matches the text? The LPS table knows. It records, for every pattern prefix, the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix — exactly the amount of re-usable progress.

How it works

  1. Build lps[] for the pattern with a two-pointer scan: extend on a match, fall back to lps[j - 1] on a mismatch.
  2. Scan the text with one pointer; on a mismatch, set j = lps[j - 1] instead of restarting. The text pointer never moves backward.
  3. On a full match, report i - m + 1 and continue from lps[j - 1] so overlapping occurrences are found too.

Worked example

Pattern ABABCABAB has lps [0, 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4]. On a mismatch after matching ABCAB, the table says the last AB still matches, so scanning resumes from there instead of re-reading the text. Over the whole scan, j rises at most n times and falls at most n times — that amortisation is the O(n + m) proof.

Key insight

Naive matching degrades to O(n x m) on inputs like AAAAAAAA with pattern AAAAB because every position restarts the comparison; the LPS table breaks that cycle with worst-case O(n + m) and no input-dependent surprises. The same failure-function idea powers Aho-Corasick (many patterns at once) and the period/rotation checks used in competitive programming.

use: Single-pattern search where worst-case guarantees matter (repetitive text is adversarial for naive search)
Streaming or one-pass matching where backtracking the input is impossible or expensive
Finding every occurrence, including overlapping ones, in linear total time
avoid: Several patterns sharing prefixes — Aho-Corasick generalises KMP for that
Very short patterns and short texts, where the naive scan is simpler and just as fast
When a battle-tested library search (two-way, Boyer-Moore variants) is a call away

commonMistakes.mistake: Building the LPS table wrongly by treating it as the longest prefix that is also a suffix — the word proper matters: lps[i] can never equal i + 1, because the whole prefix is not proper.
commonMistakes.fix: Two-pointer construction: prove it on AAAA, which must give [0, 1, 2, 3], not [1, 2, 3, 4].

commonMistakes.mistake: Moving the text pointer backward on a mismatch — that is the naive algorithm again, and the O(n x m) worst case returns.
commonMistakes.fix: Keep i fixed; fall back with j = lps[j - 1] (or 0 when j was already 0) and continue at the same text position.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stopping after the first match, or restarting from j = 0 on a match, so overlapping occurrences are missed — ABA occurs twice in ABABA.
commonMistakes.fix: On a match, record the start index and resume from j = lps[j - 1] so the overlapping suffix state is preserved.

name: Rabin-Karp
description: Hashes every text window with a rolling hash and verifies character-by-character only when a window's hash matches the pattern's. Its real strength is searching many patterns at once.
explanation:
What it is

Rabin-Karp turns string comparison into number comparison. Each m-length window's hash is computed from the window before it in O(1) — drop the leading character, shift the rest, add the trailing one — so the scan costs O(n) hash updates plus verification on suspected matches.

How it works

  1. Hash the pattern and the first text window with a polynomial hash modulo a large prime.
  2. Slide: h = (h - leading x d^(m-1)) x d + trailing, all modulo p.
  3. Whenever window and pattern hashes match, verify character-by-character before reporting — hashes can collide.
  4. For k patterns, hash them all once and compare each window against the hash set.

Worked example

Pattern ABABCABAB, text ABABDABACDABABCABAB: the window hash matches at the true start and also at the false start ABABD (the first four characters agree), where verification rejects it. The expected number of verifications stays small when the modulus spreads hashes well.

Key insight

Expected O(n + m) with uniformly distributed hashes; worst case O(n x m) when every window collides — and an adversary who knows the modulus can arrange that. Choosing a large prime (10^9 + 7, or 2^61 - 1 with overflow-safe arithmetic) keeps collisions rare in practice; double hashing or verification makes the guarantee real. The multi-pattern trick — one hash set, one pass — is why plagiarism detectors and k-gram similarity tools build on it.

use: Searching many patterns in one pass (hash them all, check the set per window)
Multi-pattern similarity: plagiarism detection, winnowing, k-gram fingerprinting
Streaming windows where updating a rolling hash beats re-scanning
avoid: Adversarial input with a fixed modulus, where collisions can be engineered
Single-pattern search where KMP gives a clean worst-case guarantee for the same effort

commonMistakes.mistake: Reporting a match on hash equality alone — collisions are rare but real, and each one becomes a false positive in the output.
commonMistakes.fix: Verify the window character-by-character (or with a second hash) before reporting.

commonMistakes.mistake: Recomputing each window's hash from scratch — that is O(m) per position, O(n x m) total, and the rolling update was the entire point.
commonMistakes.fix: Roll: h = (h - leading x d^(m-1)) x d + trailing, with d^(m-1) mod p precomputed once.

commonMistakes.mistake: A small or non-prime modulus — collisions become common and worst-case verification dominates the run.
commonMistakes.fix: Use a large prime (10^9 + 7 or 2^61 - 1) and consider double hashing when an adversary controls the input.

name: BST Insert
description: Inserts a key by walking left for smaller and right for larger values until an empty slot appears. O(log n) on balanced trees, O(n) when sorted input degenerates the tree into a list.
explanation:
What it is

A binary search tree stores keys so that everything left of a node is smaller and everything right is larger. Insert follows that invariant: compare, descend, attach. In-order traversal then visits keys in sorted order — that property is the reason BSTs exist.

How it works

  1. Compare the new key with the current node; smaller goes left, larger goes right.
  2. Repeat until the chosen child position is empty and attach the new node there.
  3. Decide the duplicate policy once — ignore, count, or place consistently — and keep search and delete consistent with it.
  4. Recursive form: return the (possibly new) subtree root from every call so the parent pointers stay intact.

Worked example

Inserting 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80 produces a perfectly balanced three-level tree; searching any key takes at most 3 comparisons. Inserting 10, 20, 30, 40 in order instead produces a chain four levels deep — search is now a linear scan.

Key insight

Average case for random insertion order is about 1.39 log2(n) comparisons; sorted or nearly-sorted input gives the O(n) worst case, visibly. Balanced variants (AVL, red-black, B-trees for disk storage) add rotations to guarantee O(log n) by construction — which is why production sorted maps use them rather than raw BSTs. In-order traversal is the sorted sequence; the invariant is the data structure's entire value proposition.

use: Dynamic ordered sets: range queries, predecessor/successor, min/max with insertions
Streaming data searched and extended repeatedly
Teaching the invariant before balanced variants take over
avoid: Sorted or adversarial insertion sequences without rebalancing — the tree becomes a list
Scale where membership only matters — a hash table is O(1) average
Static data: sort once and binary search

commonMistakes.mistake: Accidentally allowing duplicate keys: equal values walking right create silent runs of duplicates, and search returns an arbitrary one of them.
commonMistakes.fix: Choose a duplicate policy explicitly (ignore, store a count per node) and enforce it in insert, search and delete alike.

commonMistakes.mistake: Losing the tree root in the recursive insert: assigning node.left = insert(...) but forgetting to return node, so the top-level call discards the new subtree.
commonMistakes.fix: Every recursive insert returns its (possibly new) subtree root; the caller assigns it back to the tree.

commonMistakes.mistake: Feeding sorted input and assuming log-time behaviour: the walk becomes a linear scan at exactly the moment the data looks most orderly.
commonMistakes.fix: Use a self-balancing tree for sorted-heavy workloads or randomize insertion order where acceptable.

name: Heap Insert
description: Appends the new value at the end of the heap array, then sifts it up while it beats its parent. O(log n), and together with extract-max it forms the priority queue interface.
explanation:
What it is

A binary heap is a complete tree stored in an array: children of index i live at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, so no pointers are needed. Insert exploits completeness: the new element goes in the only free array slot, and sifting up restores the heap property in at most one path to the root.

How it works

  1. Append the value to the end of the array.
  2. While the index is above the root and the value exceeds its parent (parent = (i - 1) // 2), swap upward.
  3. Stop when the parent is larger, or the root is reached — the heap property now holds everywhere.

Worked example

Heap [9, 7, 8, 3, 6] and insert 10: it lands at index 5, beats its parent 8 at index 2 and swaps, then beats 9 at index 0 and swaps — two comparisons, two swaps, and 10 is the new root. Inserting 1 instead would cost zero swaps.

Key insight

Sift-up moves along a single root path, so the cost is the height of the tree, floor(log2 n) — and at most half the elements are leaves, which is why building a heap bottom-up costs O(n), not O(n log n). With extract-max (sift-down) the interface is complete: peek O(1), push and pop O(log n), all in one array. That combination powers heapsort, priority queues, Dijkstra's frontier and top-k selection.

use: Priority queues: schedulers, event simulation, Dijkstra/A* frontiers
Top-k and streaming extremes where sorting everything is wasteful
Teaching the sift-up invariant, a companion to heapsort's build phase
avoid: Ordered iteration — a heap is not sorted; use one when you need the sequence
Membership tests by value; heaps order by position, not key

commonMistakes.mistake: Using 1-based parent math on a 0-indexed array: parent is (i - 1) // 2, not i // 2, so odd-indexed elements compare against the wrong node and the heap silently violates its property.
commonMistakes.fix: Pin the layout with a unit test: children 2i + 1 / 2i + 2, parent (i - 1) // 2.

commonMistakes.mistake: Sifting up without stopping at the root (missing the i > 0 condition), so index -1 wraps around and reads the array's last element.
commonMistakes.fix: Loop while i > 0 and arr[i] > arr[(i - 1) // 2]; swapping inside the loop naturally promotes the correct chain.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mixing max-heap and min-heap comparisons between insert and extract, leaving the root unpredictable.
commonMistakes.fix: Pick one orientation, document it on the class, and use the same comparison in sift-up and sift-down.

name: BST Search
description: Walks from the root comparing the target with each node — smaller goes left, larger goes right — discarding a whole subtree with every comparison. O(log n) on a balanced tree; O(n) when sorted input has turned it into a chain.
explanation:
What it is

Search in a binary search tree is binary search that survives insertions. The ordering invariant — everything left of a node is smaller, everything right is larger — means a single comparison at each node rules out an entire subtree, so the walk follows one root-to-leaf path instead of scanning. Where a sorted array freezes at build time, the tree keeps the same logarithmic search on a growing set.

How it works

  1. Start at the root; compare the target with the node's key.
  2. Go left when the target is smaller, right when it is larger.
  3. Stop on equality — found — or at a null child, which proves the key is absent without exploring anything else.

Worked example

Tree 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80, target 60: 60 > 50 goes right to 70; 60 < 70 goes left to 60 — found in three comparisons, five nodes never touched. Searching 65 instead falls off 60's right child after the same three steps, proving absence just as cheaply.

Key insight

The cost is the height of the tree, not the count of keys: about log2(n) comparisons when balanced, n when the tree has degenerated into a chain — inserting 10, 20, 30, 40 in order builds exactly that chain. The invariant that makes search fast is the thing rebalancing schemes (AVL, red-black, B-trees) spend their rotations protecting. Against a hash table's O(1) average lookup, the BST's edge is order: predecessor, successor, min, max and range queries all fall out of the same walk.

use: Ordered lookups where predecessor, successor or range queries must stay available
Dynamic sets under mixed insert and search workloads
The search step of ordered-map implementations before rebalancing takes over
avoid: Membership-only checks at scale — a hash table does it in O(1) average
Sorted input without rebalancing — the tree becomes a list
Static data — sort once and binary search an array

commonMistakes.mistake: Recursing but discarding the return value — calling search(node.left, ...) without returning it — so every search claims the key was not found even though the walk was correct.
commonMistakes.fix: Return the recursive call; or write the loop iteratively, which makes this bug unrepresentable.

commonMistakes.mistake: A duplicate policy mismatch: insert sends equal keys one way while search stops at the first equal key coming from the other direction, leaving equal keys unreachable or inconsistently found.
commonMistakes.fix: Fix one policy — equal keys ignored, counted, or consistently sent right — and apply it in insert, search and delete alike.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pruning on comparisons in a tree that does not obey the invariant: running the BST walk over an arbitrary binary tree returns wrong answers.
commonMistakes.fix: BST search is only valid where the ordering invariant holds; validate the tree before treating it as a search tree.

name: BST In-Order Traversal
description: Recursively visits a node's left subtree, the node itself, then its right subtree — and on a binary search tree that fixed skeleton reads the keys out in sorted order. One of three visit positions that define in-order, pre-order and post-order.
explanation:
What it is

A traversal is an orderly walk of every node: recursion handles the bookkeeping, and where the visit action sits relative to the two recursive calls decides the order. In-order — left subtree, node, right subtree — is the one that makes a BST useful: it reads the tree out as a sorted sequence, which is the ordering invariant restated as an algorithm.

How it works

  1. Base case: a null node returns immediately; that is what stops the recursion.
  2. Recurse left, visit the node, recurse right. Moving the visit between the two calls yields pre-order (visit first) and post-order (visit last).
  3. Iteratively: push ancestors on the way left, pop-and-visit, then descend into the right child — the shape of a BST iterator with O(1) amortised next().

Worked example

Tree 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80. In-order gives 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80 — sorted, in three levels of recursion. Pre-order (visit first) gives 50, 30, 20, 40, 70, 60, 80 — the order that can rebuild the tree. Post-order (visit last) gives 20, 40, 30, 60, 80, 70, 50 — children before parents.

Key insight

Every node is visited exactly once — O(n) — and the auxiliary cost is the recursion depth, O(h). In-order is how a BST is validated (keys must be non-decreasing), how the k-th smallest key is extracted, and how expression trees print infix; pre-order serialises a tree for storage or copying; post-order frees it bottom-up. On a degenerate chain all three recurse n deep, which is why the iterative stack version exists: it moves the frontier from the call stack to the heap, where it can be sized and inspected.

use: Reading a BST in sorted order, or its k smallest keys with an early-stopped walk
Validating a BST: walk in-order and compare each key against the previous one
Expression trees — in-order prints infix, post-order evaluates
avoid: Deep degenerate trees with plain recursion — use the explicit-stack version
Breadth-first questions (levels, shortest depth) — those need a queue, not recursion

commonMistakes.mistake: Putting the visit in the wrong slot — visiting before the left recursion while claiming in-order — which produces output that is almost sorted, harder to spot than an outright failure.
commonMistakes.fix: Write the skeleton down as left → node → right and pin it with a fixture test on the 20..80 tree.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mutating the tree (insert or delete) while the traversal recurses, invalidating the child pointers the recursion still expects to follow.
commonMistakes.fix: Collect keys or node references first and process them afterwards, or use the explicit-stack iterator that takes each step deliberately.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming the recursion depth is safe: it equals the tree's height — n on a sorted-input chain, enough to overflow the call stack.
commonMistakes.fix: Rebalance where possible, or switch to the iterative stack, which allocates the frontier on the heap.
